question.text: Ms. Priya Shah (Company Secretary SIA) is comparing tax status across three legal forms for a new rural-skills SE. Which statement is MOST ACCURATE regarding the Income Tax treatment across Section 8 Companies, Trusts and Societies?

answer.text: All three forms — Section 8 companies, trusts and societies — must register under 12AB to claim Section 11 exemption
Only Section 8 companies can register under 12AB; trusts and societies must use Section 25
Trusts are automatically tax-exempt; only Section 8 companies and societies need 12AB registration
Section 8 companies are taxed as private limited companies and cannot access 80G status

explanation.text: **The Logic:** The chapter explicitly notes: 'NPOs take a variety of legal forms such as societies, trusts and not-for-profit companies. All NPOs must be registered under Section 12AB of the Income Tax Act and file income tax returns.' So the legal form does not change the tax-exemption route — 12AB registration plus Section 11 compliance applies uniformly, and all three can obtain 80G status. The only statutory differences are in governance (Companies Act vs Indian Trusts Act 1882 vs Societies Registration Act 1860) and in CSR-spending eligibility. **The Trap:** Section 25 is the OLD reference (Companies Act 1956) — the current equivalent is Section 8 of Companies Act 2013. Trusts are NOT automatically exempt; they need 12AB. Section 8 companies DO qualify for 80G once registered. **Cross-Exam Context:** X-A/X-B (Investment Adviser) tests legal-form comparisons when advising founders. XXIII frames it as the SIA's cross-form readiness when a funding collaborative backs SEs in all three legal forms. **Assessor's Pro-Tip:** For cross-form assessments, maintain a single working paper mapping legal form vs governance docs: Section 8 -> MoA/AoA + CSR-1; Trust -> Trust Deed + 12AB; Society -> Memorandum of Society + 12AB. This saves time on repeat engagements within a portfolio.
